title: Go through every row
summary: ws.iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True) hands you each row below the header as a tuple of values. Unpack it into names, and the loops, totals and counters from PY1 work on a spreadsheet.
objectives: Loop over a sheet’s rows with iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True).
Unpack each row into named variables.
Add up a column and count rows that match.
Find the row with the biggest value.

slides.h: By the end: the stock report in five lines
slides.say: Meera’s stock sheet will soon have 600 items. By the end of this lesson your program goes through every row, totals the stock’s value and lists what has run out, however long the sheet gets.
points: A loop over rows replaces scrolling and SUM formulas.
It works the same for 6 rows or 60,000.
p: Meera’s stock sheet will soon have 600 items. By the end of this lesson your program goes through every row, totals the stock’s value and lists what has run out, however long the sheet gets.
A loop over rows replaces scrolling and SUM formulas.
It works the same for 6 rows or 60,000.

visual.text:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True):
    item, qty, price = row
    if qty == 0:
        print("Out of stock:", item)
notes: One row at a time, below the header
Your PY1 if, on a spreadsheet

slides.say: Each round, `row` is a **tuple**: the row’s values in column order, like `("Pens", 120, 10)`. `min_row=2` skips the header. `values_only=True` gives the values instead of cell objects.
points: A tuple is like a list you can’t change.
p: Each round, `row` is a **tuple**: the row’s values in column order, like `("Pens", 120, 10)`. `min_row=2` skips the header. `values_only=True` gives the values instead of cell objects.

slides.say: `item, qty, price = row` gives each value its own name in one line. The number of names must match the number of columns, or Python stops with a ValueError.
points: Names make the code read like the sheet: `qty * price`.
Too few or too many names: “too many values to unpack”.

slides.say: The PY1 pattern, on a sheet: start at 0 before the loop, add inside it, print after it.
p: The PY1 pattern, on a sheet: start at 0 before the loop, add inside it, print after it.

visual.text:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
total = 0
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True):
    item, qty, price = row
    total += qty * price
print(f"Stock value: ₹{total}")
notes: Start at zero, before the loop
After the loop: the whole total

slides.say: Keep the best so far, and change it when a row beats it. To count, add 1 when a row matches.
points: Start `best = None` and take the first row, or start from 0 for amounts that can’t be negative.

Unpack it: `item, qty, price = row` (one name per column), or right in the for line.
Totals start at 0 before the loop, grow inside it, and print after it.
For the biggest: keep the best so far and replace it when a row beats it.

practice.prompt: Print the average price of the items, with 2 decimals, like **Average price: ₹16.67**.
practice.model:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
total, n = 0, 0
for item, qty, price in ws.iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True):
    total += price
    n += 1
print(f"Average price: ₹{total / n:.2f}")
